RagShortTexts: Following Durbe, Herkus Monte led the Great Prussian Uprising, besieging Teutonic redoubts.

Variants.Content: Spurred by its victory at Durbe in 1260, where Baltic allies inflicted a bloody defeat on the Teutonic Knights, the Great Prussian Uprising of 1260 to 1274 erupted across the Baltic provinces. Led by Herkus Monte, a Natangian chieftain who had been educated in Germany, the rebels captured siege artillery and adopted European field tactics, which let them press the Order's castles hard. They razed Teutonic outposts across the region. By the height of the revolt, only Königsberg and Elbing remained in Teutonic hands, and both were under siege. The uprising showed that the Order's conquest of Prussia was far from settled.
Monte was a nemesis forged by the Order's own schooling. Fluent in Latin, he turned European military doctrine against his former masters, restoring pagan altars in blood sacrifices.

Teutonic garrisons inside Königsberg boiled leather horse harness to stave off hunger. Only the continuous seasonal crusades proclaimed by the Pope kept the Order from being wiped out in Prussia. Each winter brought a new call to arms, and each call cost the Order treasure and men.
